clinical_knowledge.topic: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (until proven otherwise) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (until proven otherwise) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes IMMEDIATE CT head (non-contrast), IV access, analgesia (avoid NSAIDs if SAH confirmed), neurosurgical referral, LP if CT negative, strict bed rest, nimodipine if SAH confirmed, family notification, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: worst headache of my life, came on suddenly 2 hours ago

Key HPI features: thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within 1 minute, occipital and nuchal distribution, 10/10 severity, associated nausea and one vomit, mild photophobia, no focal weakness or speech problems, was lifting at the gym when it started
Objective/Exam findings: CRITICAL — immediate non-contrast CT head required within 6hrs of onset. If CT negative: LP at 12hrs post-onset for xanthochromia. Neurological exam, BP, pupils, fundoscopy.
Relevant background/PMH: no significant past medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (until proven otherwise).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Thunderclap migraine (diagnosis of exclusion) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute — the defining feature that separates this from a normal headache.
management_principles: IMMEDIATE CT head (non-contrast), IV access, analgesia (avoid NSAIDs if SAH confirmed), neurosurgical referral, LP if CT negative, strict bed rest, nimodipine if SAH confirmed, family notification
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
Provide clear patient education, address patient concerns, and establish explicit follow-up and safety-netting instructions.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 42M with sudden 10/10 thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity in <1 minute during exertion, occipital/nuchal distribution, nausea, vomiting, photophobia. No focal neuro deficit. No prior similar headache.
reference_soap.objective: CRITICAL — immediate non-contrast CT head required within 6hrs of onset. If CT negative: LP at 12hrs post-onset for xanthochromia. Neurological exam, BP, pupils, fundoscopy.
reference_soap.assessment: Subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise — MEDICAL EMERGENCY. DDx: thunderclap migraine (diagnosis of exclusion), RCVS, sentinel headache, benign exertional headache.
reference_soap.plan: IMMEDIATE CT head (non-contrast), IV access, analgesia (avoid NSAIDs if SAH confirmed), neurosurgical referral, LP if CT negative, strict bed rest, nimodipine if SAH confirmed, family notification.

learning_objectives: Recognise thunderclap headache as a neurological emergency
Apply Ottawa SAH Rule clinical assessment
Communicate urgency without catastrophising to an anxious reluctant patient
Explain why LP is needed even if CT is negative

teaching.one_liner: A sudden 'thunderclap' headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute is bleeding around the brain until proven otherwise — needs immediate CT, and if negative, a lumbar puncture, before it can be safely called anything else.
red_flags: Reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute — the defining feature that separates this from a normal headache

history.answer: Doctor, I have the worst headache of my life, and it hit me out of nowhere about two hours ago.
It came on like a lightning strike while I was lifting weights at the gym, reaching maximum intensity in less than a minute.
I have never experienced a headache like this before, and I rarely ever get headaches at all.
The pain is mainly at the back of my head and spreading down across my neck.
It feels like an explosive, throbbing agony, and it is definitely a ten out of ten.
It started two hours ago and has stayed severely intense the entire time without easing up.
Moving my head or straining makes the throbbing worse, and keeping completely still in the dark helps a tiny bit.
No, I did not have any flashing lights, blind spots, or weird sensations before the pain struck.
I feel very sick to my stomach and threw up once, and the bright lights in here hurt my eyes.
No, my eyes are not watery or bloodshot, and I have no runny nose or droopy eyelid.
I haven't felt feverish and have no rash, but my neck feels stiff and hurts to bend.
No, I have not had any limb weakness, numbness, slurred speech, confusion, or seizures.
No, my vision is clear other than light sensitivity, and I don't have double vision or eye pain.
No, I have not bumped, hit, or injured my head recently.
I haven't taken any painkillers yet because the headache happened so fast.
I was straining hard during heavy barbell squats when it suddenly exploded in my head.
I do not have high blood pressure, and I do not take blood thinners or any other prescription medicine.
No one at home is sick or has a headache, and our heating is electric and working fine.
No, I have never had cancer, HIV, or any condition that affects my immune system.
I was hoping I just pulled a muscle in my neck while lifting weights.
My wife panicked and made me come straight in, but honestly hospitals make me quite anxious.
I really need strong pain relief, and I hope you can confirm that it is nothing serious.
I have always been fit and healthy with no significant medical problems.
I have never had any surgeries or stays in a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or dietary supplements.
I have no known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine products.
I drink around fifteen units of alcohol a week, mostly a couple of beers after work on weekends.
I work as a builder, and I live with my wife and our two young children.
There is no family history of brain aneurysms, brain hemorrhages, strokes, or severe headaches.

exam.finding: Patient appears in acute distress, lying still with eyes closed and holding the back of his head.
Blood pressure is 158/92 mmHg, pulse 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light, visual fields are full, and fundoscopy reveals sharp optic disc margins with no papilledema or subhyaloid hemorrhage.
No tenderness upon percussion or palpation over the frontal and maxillary sinuses bilaterally.
Mild tenderness and palpable spasm over the posterior cervical and suboccipital musculature without midline bony spinal tenderness.
Marked resistance and pain on passive flexion of the neck, while Kernig and Brudzinski signs are absent.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with normal extraocular movements and no facial asymmetry.
Muscle bulk and tone are normal with 5/5 strength throughout all four extremities.
Sensation to light touch and pinprick is completely intact and symmetric in all limbs.
Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally with bilateral flexor plantar responses.
Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing are normal, and gait is stable without ataxia.
